title: Nights, weekends and Claude: Tailout: basement slot car racing is live. Thoughts and processes of a first-time solo dev.
author: RocketGruntJake
selftext:
Hey all. I just launched Tailout, a slot car racing game set in an '80s basement. One trigger: squeeze to go, lift for the bends, push too hard and you fly off the track. It's free on itch.io for Windows and Mac: https://daddio-retro.itch.io/tailout



Quick background: I've got a day job as business analyst, so this was nights and weekends and an entirely new experience for me. It's built in Unity and C#, plus a .NET server for online rooms. Claude Opus 5.5 wrote essentially all of the code, the art pipeline scripts and even the trailer. I directed, playtested and made the calls to get to the final product based on the vision of an online slot car simulator with a very distinct setting to play with my dad and brothers. The prompting wasn't really the secret sauce, though. The workflow was.



The big one was Solo Queue, a project board I had Claude build early on. It lives in the project folder and Claude reads it every session. Every change it makes gets logged against the part of the game it touched and turns into a "confirm" card. Claude runs whatever checks it can (tests, builds, renders), then leaves me the hands-on part, like "race a lap and see if the car flies off on this bend." Nothing's done until I've actually tried it, which pretty much killed the "it said it fixed it" problem. Anything that's my call, like taste, money, prices or anything public, comes up as a decision card with a recommendation, and Claude moves on to other work while I answer it from my phone. In the current project state we are working on Task 548 with many more planned.



The online side was a fun one. The rooms run on a small VPS: a .NET server in Docker, with four-letter room codes. Since that server costs money every month, online is pay what you like. The game itself is free, but online unlocks with any payment on itch. The gate took some thought. You paste your itch download key into the game, and the server (not the game, so the API key never ships) checks it with itch's API. The catch is that on a free itch page, anyone who claims the free download also gets a key. So for any key tied to an account, the server also asks itch whether there's an actual payment over $0 behind it. One payment covers two accounts, so you and a friend. And today I added giveaway keys: keys from my own key groups carry a prefix the server recognizes, so they unlock even after someone claims them on itch.



A couple of other bits. The cars started as image-model concepts, went through Meshy image-to-3D, and Blender scripts put the bodies, wheels and paint masks together. The trick to making five cars look like one boxed set was a "style lock" prompt kit that spells out what to match from the first car (finish, panel lines, chipping) and what NOT to copy (the silhouette). The trailer is basically code too: the game records takes, a Python script cuts them from a shot list, the title cards are HTML rendered in a headless browser, and ffmpeg stitches it all together. My edit notes were things like "the crash at :46 clips into the bridge, swap it."



What AI was bad at: feel. Claude can't tell if a trigger feels twitchy, so the driving and tuning took the most hands-on iteration by far.



\*\*Playtesters wanted!\*\* If you're into racing games, couch co-op or just want to poke at the online setup, comment or DM me and I'll send a free online key. Each one unlocks two accounts, so bring a friend. I'm especially looking for feedback on how online feels (lag, disconnects, weirdness) and whether the driving clicks for slot racing newbies and veterans alike.



Happy to go deeper on any of this. And looking forward to racing some of you online!
